title: Evaluation of Biomaterials for Bladder Augmentation using Cystometric Analyses in Various Rodent Models
protocol: Set up the sterile surgical field with necessary instruments.
Anesthetize the animal with isoflurane inhalation in the induction chamber.
Confirm complete induction before transferring to the surgical field.
Position the animal supine on the sterile drape.
Remove fur from the lower abdomen using shaving shears.
Prep the abdomen with betadine and 70% ethanol.
Inject an analgesic such as buprenorphine subcutaneously for pain control.
Make a 1-2 cm midline incision with a scalpel through the skin.
Deepen the incision at the lower portion through the rectus muscle carefully.
Elevate the rectus muscle using toothed forceps.
Dissect free the posterior surface of the muscle with fine Metzenbaum scissors.
Incise the remainder of the muscle in the midline for the entire length of your skin incision.
Deliver the bladder through the incisional wound.
Place one stay suture through the posterior wall of the bladder using 6-0 polypropylene suture.
Place another stay suture through the anterior wall of the bladder using 6-0 polypropylene suture.
Place additional sutures laterally on the bladder.
Incise the bladder longitudinally through the anterior wall in the midline for approximately 1 cm.
Trim the silk scaffold to the approximate area of the bladder defect using fine scissors.
Start at one corner of the scaffold and suture it to the bladder using 7-0 polyglactin suture.
Create a continuous, running fashion watertight seal all the way around the defect.
Test the integrity of the anastomosis by filling the bladder with sterile saline through the wall of the bladder with a 30 gauge hypodermic needle.
Close any leaks found with additional interrupted 7-0 polyglactin sutures.
Reduce the reconstructed bladder back into the abdomen.
Inject the rectus muscle and subcutaneous tissue with bupivicaine for local anesthesia (less than 3 mg/kg of 0.25%).
Reapproximate the rectus muscle with a continuous, running 4-0 polyglactin suture.
Close the skin with a continuous, running 4-0 polyglactin suture.
Clean and dry the incision.
Transfer the animal into a warm, clean cage for awakening from anesthesia.
Flare the end of the PE-50 tubing by gently exposing it to a flame.
Anesthetize the animal as described in step 1.2.
Remove the fur from both the dorsum between the scapula and the lower abdomen with shaving shears.
Prep the areas with betadine followed by 70% ethanol.
Place the animal prone on the drape.
Make a 1 cm incision on the dorsum between the scapula.
Develop a plane between the skin and the underlying muscle using Metzenbaum scissors.
Reposition the animal supine.
Make an abdominal incision to expose the bladder as described in steps 2.1-2.4.
Reduce the bladder back into the abdomen.
Place a small clamp into the subcutaneous tunnel created earlier starting from the dorsal skin incision.
Pierce through the abdominal wall with the tips of the clamp into the abdomen using fingers to protect intra-abdominal contents.
Grasp the smooth end of the PE-50 tubing with the clamp and pull it back through the dorsal incision.
Ensure that the bulbed end is not pulled past the abdominal wall.
Deliver the bladder through the incision.
Handle the bladder with fine forceps to prevent trauma.
Note the proposed site for the cystostomy tube at the dome of the bladder.
Place a pursestring stitch at the dome of the bladder using 6-0 polypropylene suture.
Start the first throw of the suture through the wall of the bladder longitudinally, lateral to the proposed site.
Leave a small clamp on the loose end of the suture.
Place the next throw in a transverse direction, starting slightly lateral to the exit of the first throw.
Do not pull the suture taut.
Place your next suture parallel to your first, going into the bladder just cephalad to the exit site of your last transverse suture.
The fourth throw will start lateral to the exit of the last stitch and end next to the entrance for your very first throw.
Pierce the bladder wall in the center of the pursestring suture using an 18G needle.
Place the tips of fine forceps into the opening and gently spread to widen the hole.
Insert the bulbed end of the catheter into the defect until it is intraluminal.
Pull the pursestring suture tight around the catheter and tie it down.
Take one end of the suture and wrap it around the catheter once, then tie it down.
With a 1 mL syringe and 25G needle, insert the needle into the tubing and slowly inject saline to distend the bladder.
Observe for leaking around the catheter.
Once leaking from the urethra is observed, aspirate the saline to decompress the bladder again.
Close the abdominal incision as above in steps 4.1-4.4.
Reposition the animal prone.
CloseOperationstheDorsalIncisionSecuringtheCatheter(ForRats)
Cut the catheter tubing at the level of the skin with scissors.
Insert a 22G blunt tip needle into the tubing.
Close the skin over the tubing with 4-0 polyglactin in a running fashion.
Leave the needle hub extruding from the skin.
Place an intravenous line cap on the blunt needle.
Secure the catheter tip to the skin using 3-0 silk suture.
Clean the incision.
Transfer the rat into a warm, clean cage for awakening from anesthesia.
Occlude the distal end of the catheter by kinking it or using a flame to melt the end.
Coil the end of the tubing and leave it in the subcutaneous pouch on the dorsum of the animal without cutting it.
Close the skin over the tubing with 4-0 polyglactin in a running fashion.
On the day of cystometry, prepare the dorsal incision with betadine and 70% ethanol.
Open the dorsal incision under anesthesia.
Remove the coiled tubing from the subcutaneous pouch.
Close the incision.
Awaken the animal from anesthesia.
Perform cystometry when the animal is fully awake.
Administer subcutaneous injections of meloxicam (0.5-1.0 mg/kg) daily for the first 3 days post-operatively.
Provide buprenorphine (0.05-0.1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 8-12 hours) as needed.
Monitor animals 3 times daily for the first 3 days, twice daily on days 4 to 5, and then once a day thereafter.
Administer Baytril (5mg/kg subcutaneous every 24 hr in a volume not exceeding 0.1 mL) for the first 72 hours post-surgery.
Wait at least 5-7 days before conducting cystometric analysis to allow bladder healing and decreased inflammation.
Calibrate volume and pressure based on the specifications of the cystometric system used.
Place animals in metabolic cages suspended over a scale connected to a transducer.
Purge the system of air bubbles.
Connect data capture system to a computer and observe for data tracings.
Adjust the scale accordingly.
Access suprapubic catheters with a 27G needle connected via a T-tube to the pressure transducer and infusion pump.
Begin infusion of physiologic saline at 12.5 μL/min for mice or 100 μL/min for rats.
Allow voiding pattern tracing to stabilize, which usually takes approximately 10-20 minutes.
Record micturition cycles for 45-120 minutes or at least 3-4 voiding cycles.
Observe the entire procedure in real-time to troubleshoot complications such as catheter kinking or obstruction.
Stop infusion and disconnect the catheter from the system.
Return the animal to its cage.
Anesthetize the animal with urethane (1-2 g/kg) intraperitoneally.
Expose the bladder according to steps 1.3-2.4.
Calibrate the system as in step 9.2.
Prepare the system as described in steps 9.4-9.5.
Insert a 27G needle connected via a T-tube to the pressure transducer and infusion pump into the lateral aspect of the bladder.
Record micturition cycles for 45-90 minutes.
Stop the infusion after recording.
Remove the needle from the bladder.
Euthanize the animal.
